comm.label: Communication
comm.description: speaks clearly and fluently at a steady pace, with confidence and good expression

levels.1: Hard to follow: disorganised, very short or rambling, little sense of the listener.
levels.3: Clear enough with some structure; mostly relevant; uses a reasonable share of the time.
levels.5: Clear, well organised and engaging from start to finish; signposts points, adapts language to the listener and finishes on time.

equity.label: Equity
equity.description: aware of fairness, social justice and human rights in health; can explain at an introductory level how systemic discrimination (racism, sexism, ableism) and social determinants create and maintain inequities

levels.1: Does not notice unfairness, or blames individuals for structural problems.
levels.3: Recognises that some groups are affected more and names one or two causes.
levels.5: Explains several structural causes (discrimination, social determinants, access), who is affected and why, and suggests fair, practical responses.

ethics.label: Ethical reasoning
ethics.description: sees more than one side of an issue and applies ethical principles with integrity to reach a fair, reasoned position

levels.1: Gives a one-sided or unreasoned view; misses the dilemma.
levels.3: Identifies the main dilemma and considers more than one side.
levels.5: Weighs competing principles and stakeholders fairly, reaches a reasoned position and acknowledges its limits.

critical.label: Critical thinking
critical.description: identifies the real issue, analyses it, draws logical unbiased conclusions and builds a structured, persuasive argument

levels.1: Restates the question or makes assertions without reasons.
levels.3: Identifies the main issue and gives some reasons and examples.
levels.5: Analyses the issue in depth, weighs evidence and trade-offs, and builds a logical, persuasive argument.

cultural.label: Cultural safety and self-reflection
cultural.description: recognises how their own culture and background shape their view, respects other perspectives and is willing to learn from them

levels.1: Shows little awareness of their own perspective or of other cultures; may stereotype.
levels.3: Shows some awareness that culture and background shape views; respectful.
levels.5: Reflects honestly on their own culturally shaped perspective, shows genuine respect and curiosity about others, and links this to safe care.

team.label: Teamwork and leadership
team.description: draws on real experience of diverse teams: taking initiative, building trust, handling conflict, shared accountability

levels.1: No concrete example, or describes teamwork only in general terms.
levels.3: Gives a relevant example with a clear role and some reflection.
levels.5: Gives a specific example showing initiative, trust-building, handling conflict and shared accountability, with clear lessons learned.

resilience.label: Resilience and motivation
resilience.description: handles setbacks constructively, shows determination for a health career, a growth mindset and deliberate self-care

levels.1: Little evidence of coping or motivation; vague or unrealistic.
levels.3: Describes a real challenge and reasonable coping or motivation.
levels.5: Shows realistic understanding of challenges, specific coping and self-care strategies already used, growth from setbacks and well-grounded motivation.

flex.label: Flexible problem solving
flex.description: thinks fluently, combines ideas in new ways and suggests creative, practical solutions

levels.1: No solutions, or only one obvious idea.
levels.5: Generates several creative, practical ideas, adapts when considering new angles and is open to changing their mind.

stations.title: The cost of a GP visit
stations.scenario: Surveys in Aotearoa New Zealand regularly find that some adults put off seeing a GP because of the cost of an appointment.
stations.question: Which groups are most likely to be affected, and what could be done about it?
keyPoints: Identifies groups: low-income households, Māori and Pacific whānau, people with disabilities or chronic illness, rural people, students, those with insecure work
Explains causes beyond price: time off work, transport, enrolment barriers, past experiences of discrimination
Impacts: delayed diagnosis, more emergency department use, worse chronic disease control, widening inequity
Solutions at several levels: targeted funding, low-cost or community clinics, nurse-led and pharmacy care, outreach, telehealth
Weighs trade-offs such as limited funding and workforce shortages
Clear structure: groups, then causes, then impacts, then solutions

stations.title: Hard to reach
stations.scenario: Many clinics, health websites and booking systems are difficult to use for people who are Deaf, blind, neurodivergent or have a learning disability.
stations.question: What inequities can this create, and how might health services respond?
keyPoints: Recognises ableism and how inaccessible systems create unequal access and outcomes
Examples: missed information, consent not truly informed, missed appointments, reliance on family to interpret
Links to rights: equal access, dignity, and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
Solutions: NZ Sign Language interpreters, Easy Read, accessible websites, longer appointments, staff training
Co-design with disabled people ("nothing about us without us")
Shows reflection on own assumptions about disability

stations.title: Opt-out organ donation
stations.scenario: Some countries automatically register adults as organ donors unless they choose to opt out. In New Zealand, people currently choose whether to be a donor, and families are involved in the final decision.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on New Zealand moving to an opt-out system?
keyPoints: Recognises the dilemma: saving lives vs bodily autonomy and consent
Arguments for: more donors, fewer deaths on waiting lists, reflects most people's stated wishes
Arguments against: presumed consent is not real consent, trust, family distress, uneven public awareness
Cultural perspectives, including tikanga Māori views on the body and whānau decision-making
Considers evidence: opt-out alone may not raise rates without infrastructure and family conversations
Reaches a reasoned position while respecting other views

stations.title: Paying blood donors
stations.scenario: In some countries, people are paid to donate blood plasma. In New Zealand, blood and plasma donors are volunteers and are not paid.
stations.question: Should people be paid to donate blood or plasma?
keyPoints: Identifies the dilemma: supply and self-sufficiency vs exploitation and altruism
Risk that payment targets people on low incomes, creating unfair pressure
Safety concerns: people may hide risk factors to get paid
Benefits: more supply, less reliance on imported products (NZ already imports some immunoglobulin)
Middle options: reimbursing costs or time, recognition schemes
Clear, reasoned conclusion that acknowledges the other side

stations.title: AI in the consulting room
stations.scenario: Some GP clinics now use AI tools that listen to the consultation and write the doctor's notes automatically, so the doctor can focus on the patient.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on using AI in this way?
keyPoints: Benefits: more eye contact and time with patients, less burnout from paperwork
Risks: errors in notes, privacy and data security, where recordings are stored
Consent: patients must know and be able to say no
Equity and culture: accents, te reo Māori, data sovereignty
Accountability: the clinician must still check and own the notes
Forms a balanced opinion; open to changing it with evidence

stations.title: Vaping at school
stations.scenario: Vaping has become common among secondary school students in Aotearoa New Zealand, even though vapes cannot legally be sold to anyone under 18.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on how this issue should be addressed?
keyPoints: Recognises tension: vaping helps some adults quit smoking but harms and addicts young people
Why youth vape: flavours, marketing, peer use, stress, easy supply
Unequal impact on some communities and lower-income areas
Mix of solutions: enforcement on retailers, product rules (e.g. the 2025 ban on disposable vapes), education young people trust, quit support
Involve young people and whānau in designing responses
Forms and justifies an opinion without needing deep technical knowledge

stations.title: Fifteen years from now
stations.scenario: Training to become a health professional takes many years, and careers often change direction along the way.
stations.question: Where do you see yourself in fifteen years, and how will you look after your own wellbeing along the way?
keyPoints: Realistic goals linked to genuine motivation and community need
Openness to change; aware the path may shift
Specific, practical self-care strategies already used, not just intentions
Support networks: whānau, friends, mentors, faith or culture, peer support
Awareness of burnout risk in health careers
Communicates with warmth and clarity

stations.title: A role model
stations.scenario: Most people who choose a health career can point to someone who influenced them.
stations.question: Think of a health professional you have met or learned about. What qualities do you admire in them, and how do those qualities connect to the career you want?
keyPoints: A specific person with concrete details, not a generic description
Qualities named and illustrated with behaviour seen
Honest reflection on which qualities they already have and which they need to develop
Links clearly to their own motivation and career choice
Avoids idealising; aware no professional is perfect
Clear structure: who, what they did, why it matters to me

stations.title: Your hardest trait
stations.scenario: Everyone has qualities that others can find difficult to work with.
stations.question: Describe one of yours. How do you manage it, and how might it help or hinder you as a health professional?
keyPoints: Names a genuine trait, not a disguised strength like "I work too hard"
Specific example of when it caused a problem
Concrete strategies used to manage it, and evidence they work
Recognises where the trait can also be a strength
Links to teamwork and patient care in a health setting
Shows honesty and self-awareness without being self-critical

stations.title: What shaped you
stations.scenario: Our families, cultures, communities and experiences shape how we see the world.
stations.question: What has most shaped the person you are today, and how might it influence the way you care for patients?
keyPoints: A specific influence explained with examples
Reflects on own culture or background and how it shapes their views
Recognises possible blind spots or biases it creates
Links to caring for patients from different backgrounds
Shows respect for perspectives different from their own
Authentic, well-structured story

stations.title: A respectful disagreement
stations.scenario: In health care, team members sometimes disagree about the right course of action.
stations.question: Describe a time you disagreed with someone you respected. What happened, how did you handle it, and what did you learn?
keyPoints: A real, specific situation with clear context
Explains their own view and genuinely tries to understand the other person's
Respectful communication: listening, timing, choosing the right setting
Outcome, including compromise or changing their own mind
What they learned about teamwork or themselves
Does not portray the other person negatively

stations.title: Giving back
stations.scenario: Many health professionals were involved in their communities before they started training.
stations.question: Describe a time you helped your community or someone outside your family. What did you learn about the people you were helping?
keyPoints: A specific experience with their real role and actions
Learning about the people helped, not just about themselves
Awareness of the barriers or inequities those people face
Respect and avoiding a saviour framing
Teamwork with others involved
Links to how this shapes them as a future health professional

stations.title: The life expectancy gap
stations.scenario: On average, Māori in Aotearoa New Zealand live several years less than non-Māori.
stations.question: What factors contribute to this gap?
keyPoints: Structural determinants: colonisation, land loss, income, housing, education, employment
Racism in the health system and wider society, including institutional racism
Access barriers: cost, distance, culturally unsafe services
Te Tiriti o Waitangi: Crown obligations of partnership, equity and active protection
Avoids blaming individual lifestyle choices
Mentions strengths-based approaches: kaupapa Māori services, Māori health workforce

stations.title: By Māori, for Māori
stations.scenario: Kaupapa Māori health services are designed and delivered by Māori, using Māori values, practices and models of health such as Te Whare Tapa Whā.
stations.question: How might services like these improve health outcomes for Māori?
keyPoints: Explains holistic models such as Te Whare Tapa Whā: taha tinana, hinengaro, wairua, whānau
Trust and cultural safety lead to better engagement and earlier care
Whānau-centred care and tino rangatiratanga (self-determination)
Links to Te Tiriti and equity
Considers challenges: funding, workforce, how mainstream services must also change
Reflects on own cultural position and learning

stations.title: Far from a birthing unit
stations.scenario: Several small rural maternity units in Aotearoa New Zealand have closed over the years. Some women now travel more than an hour to give birth.
stations.question: What inequities can this create, and how might they be reduced?
keyPoints: Identifies who is most affected: rural, low-income, Māori and Pacific whānau, people without a car
Risks: births on the roadside, delayed emergency care, stress, cost of travel and accommodation
Wider impacts: separation from whānau and support networks, lost local workforce
Recognises why units close: workforce shortages, safety with low birth numbers, funding
Solutions: midwife-led local care, transport and accommodation support, telehealth, rural workforce incentives
Balances safety, cost and access rather than one simple answer

stations.title: The child interpreter
stations.scenario: Patients who don't speak English well are sometimes asked to use a family member, occasionally a child, to interpret during health appointments.
stations.question: What problems can this cause, and what should health services do?
keyPoints: Accuracy: medical terms mistranslated, information filtered or softened
Confidentiality and privacy: patient may not disclose sensitive issues
Burden and harm to children who hear distressing information
Consent may not be truly informed; a breach of the right to effective communication
Solutions: professional interpreters (in person, phone, video), translated materials, staff training
Respects the patient's choice while making professional interpreting the default

stations.title: Health goes online
stations.scenario: More health services are moving online, including booking appointments, video consultations, repeat prescriptions and viewing test results.
stations.question: Who could be left behind, and how should services make sure they are not?
keyPoints: Groups at risk: older people, people on low incomes, rural areas with poor internet, disabled people, those with low digital literacy or limited English
Benefits for others: convenience, less travel and time off work
Risk of widening inequity if online becomes the only option
Solutions: keep phone and in-person options, free Wi-Fi or data, help from staff or community workers, accessible design
Co-design with users who struggle most
Weighs efficiency gains against fairness

stations.title: Taken seriously
stations.scenario: Research from several countries suggests that women's pain is more likely than men's to be underestimated by health professionals, and that conditions such as endometriosis can take years to diagnose.
stations.question: Why might this happen, and what could be done about it?
keyPoints: Explains bias: stereotypes about women and pain, research historically based on men
Recognises intersecting factors such as ethnicity, disability and class
Impacts: delayed diagnosis, suffering, loss of trust, time off school or work
Solutions: education about bias, listening and believing patients, better research, clear referral pathways
Self-reflection: how their own assumptions might affect how they listen
Structured argument supported by reasons, not just opinion

stations.title: What's on the corner
stations.scenario: Lower-income neighbourhoods in New Zealand often have more fast-food outlets and fewer affordable fresh-food options than wealthier areas.
stations.question: How might this affect people's health, and whose responsibility is it to address it?
keyPoints: Links food environment to obesity, diabetes, heart disease and dental decay
Avoids blaming individuals; explains how cost, time and access shape choices
Considers several responsibilities: government, councils, food industry, schools, communities, individuals
Possible actions: zoning near schools, healthy food subsidies, community gardens, food in schools programmes
Recognises the tension between personal freedom and public health
Reaches a reasoned view on shared responsibility

stations.title: A welcoming clinic
stations.scenario: Surveys in New Zealand show that rainbow (LGBTQIA+) young people report poorer wellbeing than their peers and are less likely to feel comfortable accessing health care.
stations.question: What might contribute to this, and how could health services become more welcoming?
keyPoints: Contributing factors: stigma, discrimination, bullying, family rejection, minority stress
Health system barriers: assumptions, wrong names or pronouns, past negative experiences
Respect and confidentiality as foundations of trust
Practical changes: inclusive forms and language, staff training, visible signals of safety, youth-friendly services
Involve rainbow young people in designing services
Reflects on own assumptions and learning

stations.title: Should parents be told?
stations.scenario: In New Zealand, people aged 16 and over can consent to their own health care, and younger people can often consent if they understand what is involved. Their information is usually kept confidential, even from their parents.
stations.question: Should parents always be told when their 14-year-old sees a doctor?
keyPoints: Identifies the tension: young person's autonomy and privacy vs parents' role and protection
Confidentiality encourages young people to seek help they might otherwise avoid
Limits: serious risk of harm can justify sharing information
Encouraging the young person to involve whānau where safe
Considers different family and cultural expectations
Reaches a nuanced position rather than "always" or "never"

stations.title: A matter of conscience
stations.scenario: Since 2021, adults in New Zealand who meet strict criteria can request assisted dying. Health practitioners can choose not to take part because of their own beliefs.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on health professionals being able to opt out of some kinds of care for personal reasons?
keyPoints: Respects the professional's conscience and moral integrity
Weighs this against patients' rights to lawful care and timely access
Recognises access problems if many practitioners opt out, especially in rural areas
Duty to tell patients how to access care elsewhere without delay or judgement (in NZ, an objecting practitioner must tell the person they can contact the SCENZ Group)
Acknowledges diverse religious, cultural and personal views
Clear position that recognises both sides; not judged on which view they hold

stations.title: Should the family know?
stations.scenario: A genetic test shows a patient carries a gene variant that greatly raises the risk of a serious but often preventable cancer. The same variant may be present in their brothers and sisters. The patient does not want them told.
stations.question: What are your thoughts?
keyPoints: Identifies conflict: patient confidentiality and autonomy vs preventing serious harm to relatives
Explores why the patient may not want to share: fear, family conflict, guilt
Preferred approach: support and encourage the patient to tell family, offer help to do so
Recognises that disclosure without consent is a serious step needing strong justification and senior advice
Considers trust in the health system if confidentiality is broken
Balanced, reasoned conclusion

stations.title: One budget, two programmes
stations.scenario: A health service can fund only one of two programmes: an expensive new medicine that extends life by several months for a small number of people with advanced cancer, or a falls-prevention programme for hundreds of older people.
stations.question: How should decisions like this be made?
keyPoints: Recognises scarce resources mean every choice has an opportunity cost
Considers principles: benefit to the most people, fairness, need, quality of life, cost-effectiveness
Hears both sides: value of extra time at end of life vs preventing injury and loss of independence
Equity: who benefits and who misses out
Fair process: transparent criteria, evidence, public and patient input (e.g. Pharmac-style decisions)
Forms a reasoned view while respecting that people weigh values differently

stations.title: Doctors on social media
stations.scenario: Some health professionals post videos about their work on social media, sometimes sharing patients' stories with permission. Their videos can reach thousands of people.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on this?
keyPoints: Benefits: public health education, countering misinformation, making careers visible
Risks: privacy even with consent, patients feeling pressured to agree, identification from details
Professionalism and trust in the profession
Conflicts of interest: sponsorship, chasing views
Possible boundaries: professional guidelines, no identifiable patients, accuracy
Balanced view with a reasoned conclusion

stations.title: Earning a place in the queue
stations.scenario: Some people argue that patients who continue to smoke should have lower priority for certain planned operations than patients who don't smoke.
stations.question: What are your thoughts?
keyPoints: Arguments for: smoking raises surgical risk and may reduce benefit; scarce resources
Arguments against: punishing addiction, slippery slope to other "lifestyle" judgements
Equity: smoking rates are higher in groups already facing disadvantage
Distinguishes clinical risk (a medical reason) from moral blame
Alternative: support to quit before surgery rather than exclusion
Reaches a reasoned, compassionate position

stations.title: If it's not this year
stations.scenario: Each year, many applicants who would make good health professionals are not offered a place.
stations.question: If you are not selected this year, what will you do?
keyPoints: Honest about disappointment, with a realistic response
Concrete plan: reflect on feedback, strengthen weaker areas, reapply or consider other pathways
Open to related careers and what they offer
Keeps wellbeing and support networks in mind
Shows commitment to health without making it their whole identity
Clear and composed communication

stations.title: Why this profession?
stations.scenario: Health care relies on many professions working together, including nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, midwives, kaiāwhina and doctors.
stations.question: Why have you chosen this profession over the others, and what do you know about what it is really like?
keyPoints: Specific reasons drawn from real experiences or research
Shows understanding of the day-to-day reality, not only the highlights
Respects other professions and sees medicine as part of a team
Realistic about demands: training length, workload, uncertainty
Evidence of testing the choice (volunteering, conversations, reading)
Genuine, well-structured answer

stations.title: After a mistake
stations.scenario: Every health professional will make mistakes during their career, and some will affect patients.
stations.question: How do you think you would cope after making a mistake that affected a patient?
keyPoints: Honesty and open disclosure to the patient and team
Puts patient safety first: fix the harm, report it
Learns from it: reflection, systems thinking, not just self-blame
Seeks support: supervisors, peers, wellbeing services
Recognises the emotional impact and the risk of burnout
Links to past experience of handling their own errors

stations.title: Where the need is
stations.scenario: Some areas of health care, such as rural general practice, mental health and care of older people, struggle to attract enough staff.
stations.question: Would you consider working in one of these areas? Why or why not?
keyPoints: Honest answer with real reasons, not just what sounds good
Understands why these areas are hard to staff
Recognises the equity impact of shortages on communities
Open-minded about how interests may change during training
Considers personal factors: whānau, lifestyle, support
Clear reasoning

stations.title: Switching off
stations.scenario: Many health professionals find it hard to switch off from work, and burnout is common.
stations.question: How will you balance your career with the rest of your life?
keyPoints: Specific strategies already in use (sport, music, faith, whānau, friends, rest)
Recognises early warning signs of stress in themselves
Willing to ask for help and use support services
Values relationships and identity outside work
Realistic about how demanding training is
Communicates with clarity and self-awareness

stations.title: Making a difference
stations.scenario: Imagine you have finished your training and are working in the health system.
stations.question: What is one thing you hope to change or contribute, and why does it matter to you?
keyPoints: A specific, realistic goal
Clear personal connection to the goal
Shows understanding of the problem and its causes
Practical ideas for how they would contribute, including teamwork
Recognises change takes time and persistence
Inspiring but grounded communication

stations.title: The long wait
stations.scenario: Emergency departments across New Zealand regularly report long waiting times, with some patients waiting many hours to be seen or admitted.
stations.question: What do you think causes this, and what could help?
keyPoints: Causes across the system: limited GP access, bed shortages, staffing, delayed discharges, ageing population
Recognises ED crowding is a whole-hospital and community problem
Impacts: patient harm, staff burnout, unequal effects on some groups
Solutions: urgent care and primary care access, better discharge planning, more beds and staff, triage improvements
Considers trade-offs and cost
Forms a clear opinion without needing detailed statistics

stations.title: When antibiotics stop working
stations.scenario: Infections that resist antibiotics are becoming more common around the world.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on how this problem should be tackled?
keyPoints: Explains in plain terms why resistance develops: overuse and misuse
Sources: unnecessary prescribing, patients not finishing courses, use in farming
Solutions: careful prescribing, public education, infection prevention, vaccination, surveillance
Need for new antibiotics and global cooperation
Recognises pressure on clinicians from patients who expect antibiotics
Clear, structured argument

stations.title: Health advice from influencers
stations.scenario: Many young people now get health information from social media influencers rather than from health professionals.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on this, and how should health professionals respond?
keyPoints: Recognises why influencers appeal: relatable, accessible, free
Risks: misinformation, products for sale, unrealistic body images
Not all online information is bad; some creators are accurate and reach people services miss
Responses: health professionals creating trustworthy content, teaching how to judge sources, partnering with trusted voices
Respect for young people's choices and cultures
Balanced view

stations.title: Who will staff our hospitals?
stations.scenario: New Zealand relies heavily on doctors and nurses trained overseas, while some health workers trained here move to Australia for higher pay.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on how New Zealand should address its health workforce shortages?
keyPoints: Causes: pay gaps, workload, training numbers, ageing workforce
Ethical issue of recruiting staff from countries that need them
Options: train more locally, rural and Māori and Pacific pathways, retention through pay and conditions, bonding schemes
Supporting overseas-trained staff to settle and practise safely
Long-term vs short-term solutions
Reasoned opinion

stations.title: Taxing sugary drinks
stations.scenario: Some countries tax sugary drinks to reduce obesity and tooth decay. New Zealand does not currently have a tax like this.
stations.question: Should New Zealand introduce one?
keyPoints: Arguments for: evidence from other countries of reduced consumption, revenue for health
Arguments against: hits low-income households harder, personal freedom, industry pushback
Equity: potential benefits are greatest in groups with highest consumption
Complementary measures: water in schools, labelling, marketing limits
Recognises a single tax is not a full solution
Forms and justifies a view

stations.title: Growing up online
stations.scenario: There is growing concern about the effect of social media on young people's mental wellbeing, and some countries are restricting social media for children.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on what should be done?
keyPoints: Recognises both harms (comparison, cyberbullying, sleep loss) and benefits (connection, identity, support)
Evidence is mixed and still developing
Considers options: age limits, platform responsibility, education, parental tools
Involves young people in solutions rather than only restricting them
Considers equity and practicality of enforcement
Draws on own observations thoughtfully

stations.title: A wrong assumption
stations.scenario: We all make assumptions about people based on how they look, speak or where they come from.
stations.question: Tell us about a time an assumption you made about someone turned out to be wrong. What did you learn?
keyPoints: An honest, specific example
Explains where the assumption came from
What changed their view
Insight into their own culturally shaped perspective
How they now act differently
Link to caring for diverse patients

stations.title: Your best quality
stations.scenario: The qualities that serve us well can sometimes work against us.
stations.question: What strength do others most often see in you, and when might that strength become a weakness in a health setting?
keyPoints: Names a genuine strength with an example
Thoughtful insight into how it can become a weakness
Concrete example or scenario in health care
Strategies to manage the downside
Self-aware without false modesty
Clear structure

stations.title: Feedback that changed you
stations.scenario: Health professionals receive feedback throughout their careers from patients, colleagues and supervisors.
stations.question: What is the most useful feedback you have received, and how did it change you?
keyPoints: Specific feedback and context
Honest about initial reaction
Reflection on why it was useful
Concrete changes made as a result
Continues to seek feedback
Links to lifelong learning

stations.title: When values differ
stations.scenario: Patients' beliefs and values will sometimes be very different from your own.
stations.question: Describe a value you hold strongly. How would you care for a patient whose beliefs are very different from yours?
keyPoints: Clearly describes a personal value and where it comes from
Recognises it shapes their views, which may differ from patients'
Commits to respectful, non-judgemental care
Practical approaches: listening, asking about what matters to the patient, not imposing views
Knows when to seek help from colleagues
Shows cultural humility

stations.title: Out of your comfort zone
stations.scenario: Training and working in health care regularly puts people in unfamiliar situations.
stations.question: When did you last step well outside your comfort zone, and what did it teach you about yourself?
keyPoints: A specific recent example
What made it uncomfortable
How they adapted and coped
What they learned about themselves
How that helps them in future challenges
Authentic and reflective

stations.title: What you bring
stations.scenario: Everyone's background gives them some advantages and some challenges.
stations.question: What advantages or challenges has your background given you, and how might they shape how you see your patients?
keyPoints: Honest reflection on their own circumstances
Recognises advantages they may have had, not only challenges
Understands how background shapes perspective and possible blind spots
Links to empathy for patients from different circumstances
Avoids assuming their experience is universal
Respectful and thoughtful communication

stations.title: Turning a group around
stations.scenario: Sometimes a group or team is not working well together.
stations.question: Describe a time you helped a group that was struggling. What did you do, and what happened?
keyPoints: Specific situation and why the group struggled
Their actions: listening, clarifying goals, sharing tasks, encouraging others
Handled any conflict respectfully
Honest outcome, including what did not work
Lessons about leadership and teamwork
Clear story structure

stations.title: Letting the team down
stations.scenario: Everyone lets people down at some point.
stations.question: Tell us about a time you let a team down. How did you handle it?
keyPoints: Takes real responsibility without excuses
Explains what happened and its impact on others
Actions taken to put it right
What they learned and changed
Rebuilt trust
Honest and self-aware

stations.title: Working across cultures
stations.scenario: Health care teams bring together people from many cultures and backgrounds.
stations.question: Describe a time you worked closely with people from a background very different from your own. What did you learn about working together?
keyPoints: Specific example and setting
Differences noticed and how they affected the work
How they adapted their communication
What they learned from others
Respect rather than stereotyping
Links to health care teams and patients

stations.title: Being there for someone
stations.scenario: Caring for others can be rewarding and demanding.
stations.question: Describe a time you supported someone through a difficult period. What did you learn about caring for others? (Choose an example you are comfortable sharing.)
keyPoints: A specific example the applicant is comfortable discussing
How they supported the person: listening, practical help, involving others
Respected the person's wishes and limits
Knew when to involve others or professional help
Looked after their own wellbeing
Learning that applies to caring for patients

stations.title: Caught in the middle
stations.scenario: Conflict between people in a group can affect everyone.
stations.question: Describe a time two people in a group you belonged to were in conflict. What role did you play?
keyPoints: Specific situation and what the conflict was about
Stayed fair and did not take sides unfairly
Helped communication between the two, or knew when to involve a leader
Kept the group's goals in focus
Outcome and what they would do differently

stations.title: Closing the smoking gap

stations.title: Making it happen
stations.scenario: Organising an event or project takes planning and teamwork.
stations.question: Describe an event or project you helped organise. What was your role, and what would you do differently?
keyPoints: Specific event and their role
Planning, delegation and communication
Problems that arose and how they solved them
Recognition of others' contributions
What they would change
Clear structure

stations.title: Something wasn't right
stations.scenario: Sometimes you notice a problem that others have missed.
stations.question: Describe a time you noticed a mistake or problem others had missed. What did you do?
keyPoints: Specific situation
How they checked they were right
How they raised it respectfully
Response of others and outcome
What they learned about speaking up
Link to patient safety culture

stations.title: Someone you clashed with
stations.scenario: We don't always get on with everyone we work with.
stations.question: Describe a time you had to work with someone you found difficult. How did you make it work?
keyPoints: Specific example, described fairly
Tried to understand the other person's perspective
Communication strategies used
Focus on shared goals
Outcome and what they learned
Avoids blaming

stations.title: Letting go
stations.scenario: Good leaders know when to share responsibility.
stations.question: Describe a time you handed a task or role to someone else. How did you decide to trust them, and how did it go?
keyPoints: Specific situation
Reasons for delegating
How they set the person up to succeed
Balancing support with trust
Outcome and lessons
Link to teamwork in health care

stations.title: Rongoā Māori
stations.scenario: Rongoā Māori is traditional Māori healing, which can include plant medicines, massage and spiritual practices. ACC now funds rongoā Māori as part of rehabilitation after an injury.
stations.question: How might rongoā and conventional medicine work together?
keyPoints: Respectful understanding of rongoā as a holistic system linked to whakapapa and whenua
Patient choice and cultural identity
Communication between practitioners and patients; asking about all treatments used
Safety: possible interactions, evidence, regulation
Partnership with rongoā practitioners rather than control
Reflects on own cultural position

stations.title: Language in care
stations.scenario: Some patients feel more comfortable speaking te reo Māori with health professionals.
stations.question: Why might language matter in health care, and what can health professionals do?
keyPoints: Language linked to identity, comfort, trust and understanding
Correct pronunciation of names as basic respect
Access to Māori-speaking staff or interpreters
Learning basic te reo and tikanga as a professional
Links to cultural safety and equity
Clear communication

stations.title: Found too late
stations.scenario: Māori are more likely than non-Māori to be diagnosed with some cancers at a later stage, when treatment is harder.
stations.question: What factors might explain this, and what could help?
keyPoints: Access barriers: cost, distance, time, transport
Experiences of racism and mistrust
Screening programme design and reach
Solutions: kaupapa Māori screening, outreach, whānau-centred approaches, Māori navigators
Te Tiriti obligations
Avoids blaming patients

stations.title: Caring after death
stations.scenario: In tikanga Māori, the body of a person who has died (tūpāpaku) is treated with particular care, and whānau may wish to stay with them and take them home quickly.
stations.question: How should hospitals support whānau at this time?
keyPoints: Respect for tikanga and its meaning to whānau
Practical responses: space for whānau, karakia, timely release processes, kaumātua involvement
Balancing legal requirements (such as coroner processes) with cultural needs
Staff training and Māori health services in hospitals
Compassion and communication with grieving whānau
Creative, practical solutions

stations.title: Wellbeing through identity
stations.scenario: Māori approaches to mental wellbeing often emphasise connection to whānau, whenua, culture and identity.
stations.question: How might culturally grounded approaches support Māori mental wellbeing?
keyPoints: Holistic models such as Te Whare Tapa Whā
Effects of colonisation and loss of connection on wellbeing
Strengths of identity, belonging and whānau
Kaupapa Māori services working alongside clinical care
Equity in access and outcomes
Thoughtful, respectful discussion

stations.title: Distance to care
stations.scenario: Many Māori whānau live in rural and provincial areas a long way from specialist health services.
stations.question: How could access to care be improved?
keyPoints: Barriers: distance, transport, cost, time off work, fewer local services
Ideas: mobile clinics, outreach specialists, telehealth, marae-based clinics
Partnership with iwi and Māori providers
Supporting whānau to travel and stay near hospitals
Rural Māori health workforce
Practical, creative ideas

stations.title: Racism in health care
stations.scenario: Surveys show many Māori report experiencing racism when using health services.
stations.question: How might this affect health, and what can individual health professionals do?
keyPoints: Effects: avoiding care, delayed treatment, stress, mistrust
Recognises personal, institutional and structural racism
Individual actions: self-reflection on bias, listening, respectful communication, speaking up
System actions: training, data monitoring, Māori leadership
Commitment to ongoing learning
Honest, respectful discussion

stations.title: Caring for the whole whānau
stations.scenario: Whānau-centred approaches support whole families rather than individuals, often working across health, housing, education and income.
stations.question: What are your thoughts on whānau-centred approaches compared with care focused on the individual?
keyPoints: Recognises whānau as a key unit of wellbeing in te ao Māori
Benefits: addresses root causes and shared challenges
Challenges: privacy, funding across agencies, measuring outcomes
Respecting individual wishes within whānau
Relevance for other cultures too
Reasoned comparison

stations.title: Iwi-led responses
stations.scenario: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many iwi and Māori health providers ran their own vaccination clinics and support programmes.
stations.question: What can the wider health system learn from responses like these?
keyPoints: Strengths: trust, local knowledge, flexible delivery, reaching whānau others missed
Tino rangatiratanga and partnership under Te Tiriti
Need for adequate, timely funding and data access
Building on these models beyond emergencies
Respectful, strengths-based framing
Practical lessons

stations.title: Kai and community
stations.scenario: Some marae and iwi run community gardens and kai programmes to improve whānau health.
stations.question: How might programmes like these support health beyond nutrition?
keyPoints: Benefits beyond food: connection, belonging, physical activity, skills, intergenerational learning
Links to whenua and cultural identity
Food security and cost of living
Community-led and strengths-based
How health services could support rather than control
Creative thinking

stations.title: The waiting room
stations.scenario: You volunteer on reception at a busy GP clinic. An older man has waited ninety minutes. He's upset and says he's leaving. As he stands up, he says his chest has felt tight all morning, "but it's probably nothing."
stations.question: Talk us through how you would handle this situation.
keyPoints: Safety first: chest tightness is a possible emergency, so tell a nurse or doctor immediately rather than diagnose
Acknowledge his frustration sincerely; stay calm and kind
Encourage him to stay, and respect his autonomy if he insists
Explain the delay honestly; do not promise what you cannot deliver
Stay with him or keep him in sight until clinical staff take over
Know the limits of a volunteer role; follow up and report the wait-time issue

stations.title: The silent group member
stations.scenario: You're in a four-person group assignment in your first year at university. One member, Tama, hasn't contributed anything and isn't answering messages. The deadline is in three days. The other two want to submit with Tama's name left off.
stations.question: What would you do, and why?
keyPoints: Avoid assumptions; there may be reasons (health, whānau, work, wellbeing)
Contact Tama privately and supportively before acting
Get the work done: redistribute tasks fairly so the group meets the deadline
Be honest about contributions; involve the tutor or course coordinator if it is not resolved
Do not act unilaterally or behind his back
Reflect on team processes, e.g. setting roles and check-ins early next time

stations.title: Overheard at a party
stations.scenario: A friend works part-time at a pharmacy. At a party, they tell a group of people that a well-known teacher from your old school collects a medication used to treat HIV.
stations.question: How would you respond in the moment and afterwards? What are the issues here?
keyPoints: Serious breach of confidentiality and health privacy (Health Information Privacy Code)
Harm: stigma, discrimination, damage to the teacher, loss of public trust in health services
Respond in the moment: calmly discourage further sharing, do not spread it
Talk to the friend privately and non-judgementally afterwards about why it matters
Friend may need to tell their pharmacist manager; consequences are possible
Link to medicine: confidentiality underpins trust between patients and health workers

stations.title: The first fail
stations.scenario: You studied hard for your first chemistry test at university and scored 38 percent. Most of your friends passed. You feel embarrassed and are starting to doubt whether you belong in a health programme.
stations.question: How would you respond? Tell us about a real setback you have faced and what you learned.
keyPoints: Acknowledge feelings honestly without catastrophising
Analyse the cause: study method, understanding gaps, exam technique, workload
Seek help early: lecturer, tutor, study groups, student support services
Look after wellbeing; keep perspective (one test, not a verdict)
A specific real example of a setback with actions and outcome
Shows growth: what they now do differently; links to resilience in medicine

stations.title: Explaining dialysis
stations.scenario: You are helping a family friend. Her 10-year-old daughter, Mele, is worried because her grandmother is starting dialysis next week. Mele asks you what kidneys do and why her nana needs a machine.
stations.question: Speak to Mele as if she is in front of you now.
keyPoints: Speaks directly to the child, warmly, in simple words without jargon
Clear analogy: kidneys clean the blood like a filter; dialysis does that job when they cannot
Honest without frightening; no false promises
Checks how Mele feels and what she already knows; invites questions
Offers practical reassurance: nana will be looked after; Mele can still visit and help
Suggests asking nana's nurse or doctor and involving family

stations.title: The worried parent
stations.scenario: A parent at your sports club tells you she won't vaccinate her new baby because of a video she watched online. She knows you want to study medicine and asks what you think.
stations.question: How would you respond?
keyPoints: Listen first; ask what worries her and what she saw
Respect and empathy; avoid lecturing, ridicule or arguing
Share balanced, reliable information within the limits of a student's knowledge
Suggest talking with her GP, practice nurse or Plunket nurse; offer trustworthy sources
Respect her right to decide while being clear about the evidence
Keep the relationship open; link to community health and herd immunity

stations.title: The captain's call
stations.scenario: You captain your school's volleyball team. Two senior players keep making jokes about a younger player's accent. He has recently moved from Samoa. The coach hasn't noticed, and the younger player has gone quiet at training.
stations.question: What would you do as captain?
keyPoints: Act promptly; this is racist bullying and harms wellbeing
Check in privately and supportively with the younger player first
Speak to the two players privately and clearly about impact and team values
Involve the coach or school staff; follow school processes
Build an inclusive team culture; follow up over time
Reflects on the responsibilities of leadership

stations.title: The neat graph
stations.scenario: Your lab partner changes one data point in your shared report so the graph looks cleaner. They say everyone does it and it will not change the conclusion. The report is worth 10 percent of your grade.
stations.question: What would you do?
keyPoints: Recognise it as fabrication, academic misconduct regardless of size
Talk to the partner calmly; understand the pressure they feel
Correct the data, or report the result honestly with explanation of the error
Escalate to the demonstrator or lecturer if the partner refuses; shared responsibility
Link to medicine: research integrity and patient safety depend on honest data
Avoid self-righteousness; offer support (time, help with analysis)
